intro: A text from a cousin says "¿Me lo mandas?" Four short words, and you know exactly what she wants: send it to me. A grandmother on the phone says "Sécalo bien" and "No lo pongas todavía," and a pot of rice comes out right. This unit is about the small words that carry the weight in Spanish sentences: lo, la, le, se, me, te, nos, and about the verb forms that tell someone what to do.

You will learn to replace nouns with direct and indirect object pronouns, to put them in the right place before a verb or attached to its end, and to write the accent that appears when a word grows. You will tell your daily routine with reflexive verbs, say that two people help each other, and then move on to commands: the familiar tú forms, the eight irregulars, the polite usted and ustedes forms, and let's with nosotros.

By the end you will be able to follow a recipe, give directions to a stranger in Pilsen, tell a friend not to worry, and explain why dámelo has an accent and no me lo des does not. You will also have most of the present subjunctive in your hands without knowing it yet, which is exactly where the next unit begins.
bigQuestion: How do a few small words and a handful of verb endings let Spanish say who does what to whom, and tell people what to do?

words.d: direct object pronoun — lo, la, los, las, me, te, nos; replaces what receives the action
indirect object pronoun — me, te, le, nos, os, les; to whom or for whom
what le or les becomes before lo, la, los, las: Se lo doy (I give it to him)
the gerund, the -ando / -iendo form — with an attached pronoun it takes an accent: leyéndolo
reflexive — the subject does the action to itself: me levanto, te duchas, se viste
reciprocal — each other, with nos, os or se: Nos ayudamos (We help each other)
the imperative, the command form — ¡Habla! ¡Come! ¡No hables!

words.w: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven
words.d: the eight irregular affirmative tú commands
don't talk — negative tú command: yo form, drop -o, flip the vowel, add -s
usted and ustedes commands — the flipped-vowel form, affirmative and negative

test.q: Which pronoun replaces "el sándwich" in "Preparo el sándwich"?
test.why: Sándwich is masculine singular, so the direct object pronoun is lo.

test.q: Which sentence has the correct order?
test.why: No comes first, then the pronoun, then the conjugated verb.
The pronoun attaches to the gerund and the accent keeps the stress on -cién-.

test.q: Which pronoun fits: "___ escribo una carta a mis abuelos."
test.why: Mis abuelos are the people who receive the letter, plural: les.

test.q: How do you say "I give them (las fotos) to her"?
test.why: Le becomes se before las; fotos is feminine plural.

test.q: Which form is correct for "we get dressed"?
test.why: Nos matches the nosotros ending, and nosotros keeps the stem e: vestimos.

test.q: What does "Me pongo los zapatos" mean?
test.why: Ponerse means to put on; the article los stands in for my.

test.q: What does "Mis amigos se abrazan" mean?
test.why: With a plural subject and abrazarse, se is reciprocal: each other.

test.q: Which is the affirmative tú command of dormir?
test.why: The tú command matches the él form, including the stem change: duerme.

test.q: Which is the tú command of poner?
test.why: Pon is one of the eight irregular tú commands.

test.q: Which is correct for "Give it to me" (el libro)?
test.why: Da + me + lo in one word with an accent because two pronouns attached.

test.q: Which is the negative tú command of salir?
test.why: Start from salgo, drop -o, add -as: no salgas.

test.q: Which is correct: "Don't sit there" to a friend?
test.why: Negative tú command with te in front and the flipped vowel: no te sientes.

test.q: Which is the ustedes command of venir?
test.why: Ustedes: from vengo, flip the vowel, add -n: vengan.
Vamos + nos with the -s dropped and an accent: vámonos.

write.prompt: Escribe un párrafo de 6 a 8 oraciones: describe tu rutina de la mañana con verbos reflexivos y luego dale tres consejos a un amigo con mandatos (uno afirmativo, uno negativo y uno con un pronombre). Write a paragraph in Spanish: your morning routine with reflexive verbs, then three commands of advice to a friend, one affirmative, one negative, and one with a pronoun attached or in front.
tips: Use at least four reflexive verbs from this unit, and make each pronoun match the subject.
For a negative command, start from the yo form and flip the vowel; put the pronoun before the verb.
If a pronoun attaches to an affirmative command or a gerund, check whether it needs a written accent.
Use the article, not a possessive, for parts of the body and clothes: me lavo la cara.
Read it aloud; if a sentence sounds like English word order, fix it.

title: Pronouns, Reflexives and Commands

chapters.title: Object Pronouns and Reflexives
chapters.bigQuestion: How does Spanish say who does what to whom without repeating every noun?

story.title: Exam Day, 6:40 a.m.
story.kicker: Daniela has a chemistry final at 8:00, and everything that can go wrong does.
paragraphs: Daniela's alarm rings at 6:00. She turns it off and thinks, "Cinco minutos más" (five more minutes). At 6:40 her little brother shakes her shoulder. "¡Despiértate! ¡Es tarde!" (Wake up! It's late!) She sits up fast. Her chemistry final starts at 8:00, and the bus leaves at 7:15.

She runs to the bathroom. "Me ducho en tres minutos," (I shower in three minutes) she promises herself. She showers, brushes her teeth, and gets dressed: *me ducho, me cepillo los dientes, me visto*. Every one of those verbs has a little word in front of it: me. In Spanish, when you do something to yourself, the verb says so.

In the kitchen her mother holds out a folder. "Tus apuntes. No los olvides." (Your notes. Don't forget them.) Daniela grabs them. Her mother also hands her a sandwich. "¿Me lo preparaste?" (You made it for me?) "Sí, te lo preparé anoche." (Yes, I made it for you last night.) Two tiny words, te and lo, carry a whole sentence of meaning: for you, it.

At the bus stop she checks her bag. The calculator is not there. She texts her brother: "¿Viste mi calculadora?" (Did you see my calculator?) He answers: "La tienes en la mochila, bolsillo de adelante." (You have it in the backpack, front pocket.) She looks. There it is. She did not have to write calculadora again; la did the job.

On the bus, Daniela and her friend Tomás quiz each other. "Nos ayudamos siempre," (We always help each other) Tomás says. By 7:55 she is in her seat, notes read, calculator found, sandwich half eaten. Nothing about the morning went the way she planned, and yet every small word landed exactly where it belonged.
story.think: Daniela's morning is full of tiny words: me, te, lo, la, los, nos. Which of them mean the person doing the action, and which mean someone or something else?

lessons.title: Finding the Direct Object
lessons.mainIdea: The direct object receives the action, and Spanish replaces it with lo, la, los or las.
reading: Tomás texts his sister: "¿Tienes la calculadora?" (Do you have the calculator?) She answers, "Sí, la tengo." (Yes, I have it.) The word la is standing in for la calculadora. It is a *pronombre de objeto directo* (direct object pronoun). The direct object is the noun that receives the action of the verb. Ask "what?" or "whom?" after the verb, and the answer is the direct object: I have what? The calculator.

Spanish has four third-person direct object pronouns, and they match the noun in gender and number: *lo* (him, it, masculine), *la* (her, it, feminine), *los* (them, masculine or mixed), *las* (them, feminine). "¿Compraste los boletos?" (Did you buy the tickets?) "Sí, los compré." (Yes, I bought them.) "¿Conoces a Marta?" (Do you know Marta?) "Sí, la conozco." (Yes, I know her.) People and things use the same pronouns.

The pronouns for me, you and us are easy because they never change for gender: me (me), te (you, familiar), nos (us). "Mi mamá me despierta." (My mom wakes me.) "Te llamo mañana." (I'll call you tomorrow.) "El profesor nos escucha." (The teacher listens to us.) The common English-speaker mistake is to translate it as lo every time. If the noun is feminine, it is la: la tarea (the homework) → la hago (I do it).

words.d: direct object pronoun — replaces the noun that receives the action: lo, la, los, las, me, te, nos
him or it (masculine) — Veo el libro → Lo veo (I see it)
her or it (feminine) — Veo la casa → La veo (I see it)
them — Veo los libros → Los veo; Veo las casas → Las veo
the calculator — a feminine noun, so it becomes la

look.title: Replace the Noun
look.text:
Read each sentence and find the direct object.
1. Daniela busca la calculadora. (Daniela looks for the calculator.)
2. Tomás lee los apuntes. (Tomás reads the notes.)
3. Mamá prepara el sándwich. (Mom makes the sandwich.)
4. Los estudiantes escuchan a la profesora. (The students listen to the teacher.)
Now say each one again with a pronoun: Daniela la busca. Tomás los lee...
look.prompt: Finish sentences 3 and 4 with the right pronoun. What did you check to pick lo, la, los or las?

check.q: Which pronoun replaces la tarea in "Hago la tarea"?
check.why: Tarea is feminine singular, so the direct object pronoun is la.

check.q: What does "Los conozco" mean?
check.why: Los is the direct object pronoun for a masculine or mixed plural group: them.

check.q: Which sentence uses the pronoun correctly for "the tickets"?
check.why: Boletos is masculine plural, so the direct object pronoun is los.

lessons.title: Where the Pronoun Goes
lessons.mainIdea: A direct object pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb, and no before the pronoun.
reading: In English the pronoun follows the verb: I see it. In Spanish it comes first: Lo veo. The pronoun sits directly in front of the *verbo conjugado* (conjugated verb), the verb with a person ending. "Mi hermano me despierta." (My brother wakes me.) "¿La calculadora? La tengo." (The calculator? I have it.) Nothing squeezes between the pronoun and the verb.

When the sentence is negative, *no* goes before the pronoun, not between the pronoun and the verb. "No lo tengo." (I don't have it.) "No te escucho." (I can't hear you.) English speakers often write "Lo no tengo" because English puts the negative next to the verb. Remember the order: no + pronoun + verb.

In a question the order stays the same; only the intonation and the question marks change. "¿Me escuchas?" (Are you listening to me?) "¿Los viste?" (Did you see them?) Subject pronouns, when they appear, go before everything: "Yo no la conozco." (I don't know her.) Say the chain out loud a few times until it feels natural: yo no la conozco, tú no la conoces, ella no la conoce.

words.d: the conjugated verb — a verb with a person ending, like tengo or escuchas; the pronoun goes right before it
I don't have it — no comes before the pronoun, never between the pronoun and the verb
to listen — Te escucho (I'm listening to you)
to know a person or place — La conozco (I know her)

look.title: Fix the Word Order
look.text:
Each sentence has English word order. Rebuild it in Spanish order.
1. Tengo lo. (I have it.)
2. Lo no veo. (I don't see it.)
3. ¿Escuchas me? (Are you listening to me?)
4. Ella conoce no los. (She doesn't know them.)
The pattern: (subject) + no + pronoun + conjugated verb.
look.prompt: Rewrite all four. Which one was the hardest to hear as wrong, and why?

check.q: Which sentence has the correct order for "I don't have it"?
check.why: The order is no + pronoun + conjugated verb: No lo tengo.

check.q: Where does the pronoun go in "Are you listening to me?"
check.why: Me goes directly before the conjugated verb escuchas.

check.q: What does "Ella no los conoce" mean?
check.why: Los is them; ella is the subject, so she doesn't know them.

lessons.title: Attached to Infinitives and Gerunds
lessons.mainIdea: With an infinitive or a gerund the pronoun may attach to the end, and a gerund then needs a written accent.
reading: Daniela says, "Voy a leer los apuntes." (I'm going to read the notes.) With a pronoun she has two choices, and both are correct: "Los voy a leer" or "Voy a leerlos." The pronoun can go before the conjugated verb (voy) or attach to the end of the *infinitivo* (infinitive, the -ar, -er, -ir form). Attached, it is written as one word: leerlos, comprarla, verte.

The same two choices exist with the *gerundio* (gerund, the -ando / -iendo form) after estar. "Estoy leyendo los apuntes" becomes "Los estoy leyendo" or "Estoy leyéndolos." Notice the accent that appeared on leyéndolos. A gerund is stressed on the syllable before -ndo: le-YEN-do. Adding -los makes the word longer, so Spanish writes an accent to keep the stress where it was: leyéndolos, comiéndola, esperándote.

Infinitives usually do not need an accent when one pronoun attaches (leerlos, verte), because the stress already falls on the last syllable and one extra syllable does not break the rules. English speakers often forget the gerund accent, or add one to an infinitive where it does not belong. Rule of thumb: gerund + pronoun always takes an accent; infinitive + one pronoun does not.

words.d: the infinitive — the -ar, -er, -ir form; a pronoun can attach to its end: leerlos
the gerund — the -ando / -iendo form; with an attached pronoun it takes an accent: leyéndolos
reading them — gerund + pronoun, accent on the stressed syllable
to wait for — Te espero / Voy a esperarte (I'll wait for you)

look.title: Two Right Answers
look.text:
Write each sentence both ways.
1. Quiero comprar la calculadora. → La quiero comprar. / Quiero comprarla.
2. Estoy haciendo la tarea. → La estoy haciendo. / Estoy haciéndola.
3. Vamos a ver a los abuelos. → ?
4. Están escuchando la canción. → ?
look.prompt: Complete 3 and 4. Which of your four attached forms needed an accent, and why?

check.q: Which is a correct way to say "I'm reading them"?
check.why: The pronoun attaches to the gerund and the accent keeps the stress on -yén-.

check.q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
check.why: The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or attached to the infinitive, never in the middle.

check.q: Why does comiéndola have an accent when comerla does not?
choices: Because the added syllable would move the stress off -mién-.
check.why: Adding a syllable to the gerund would shift the stress, so an accent marks the original stressed syllable.

lessons.title: To Whom and For Whom
lessons.mainIdea: The indirect object pronouns le and les mark the person who receives something, and Spanish usually adds them even when the noun is present.
reading: Daniela's mother made her a sandwich: "Le preparé un sándwich a Daniela." (I made a sandwich for Daniela.) The sandwich is the direct object, the thing made. Daniela is the *objeto indirecto* (indirect object), the person it was made for. Ask "to whom?" or "for whom?" after the verb, and you have found the indirect object.

The indirect object pronouns are me, te, le, nos, les. Only the third person differs from the direct ones: *le* (to him, to her, to you formal) and *les* (to them, to you all). They do not change for gender. "Le escribo a mi abuela." (I write to my grandmother.) "Les mando fotos a mis primos." (I send photos to my cousins.) "Te doy el libro." (I give you the book.)

Spanish often keeps both the pronoun and the noun in the same sentence: "Le preparé un sándwich a Daniela." This looks like a repeat to English speakers, but it is normal Spanish. The phrase *a Daniela* clears up who le means. Verbs of giving, telling and asking almost always take an indirect object: dar (to give), decir (to say), pedir (to ask for), mandar (to send), regalar (to give as a gift).

words.d: the indirect object — the person who receives, gets or is told something: to whom, for whom
to him, to her, to you (formal) — Le escribo (I write to him or her)
to them, to you all — Les mando fotos (I send them photos)
to give as a gift — Le regalo un libro a mi hermano (I give my brother a book)
to ask for — Te pido un favor (I ask you a favor)

look.title: Who Gets What?
look.text:
A: ¿Qué le regalas a tu mamá? (What are you giving your mom?)
B: Le regalo flores. ¿Y tú, qué les das a tus abuelos? (I'm giving her flowers. And you, what are you giving your grandparents?)
A: Les mando una tarjeta. (I'm sending them a card.)
In each line find the thing (direct object) and the person (indirect object).
look.prompt: Why does B say les and not le in the second question? What would change if the gift went to one grandfather only?

check.q: In "Le mando una foto a mi tía," what is le?
choices: The indirect object: to my aunt
check.why: Le marks the person who receives the photo, the indirect object.

check.q: Which pronoun fits: "___ escribo a mis padres."
check.why: Mis padres is plural, so the indirect object pronoun is les.

check.q: Which sentence means "I ask you for a favor"?
check.why: Te is the indirect object pronoun for you (familiar); pido is the yo form.

lessons.title: Two Pronouns Together
lessons.mainIdea: When a sentence has both pronouns, the indirect one comes first, and le or les becomes se before lo, la, los or las.
reading: "¿Me lo preparaste?" (Did you make it for me?) "Sí, te lo preparé." (Yes, I made it for you.) When both objects are pronouns, the indirect one comes first, then the direct one, and both go before the conjugated verb: me lo, te la, nos los. Think of the order as person first, thing second.

Now the twist. Spanish does not allow le lo or les la. When le or les comes right before lo, la, los or las, it changes to *se*. "Le doy el libro a Marta" becomes "Se lo doy." (I give it to her.) "Les mando las fotos a mis primos" becomes "Se las mando." (I send them to them.) This se is not reflexive; it is just le or les in disguise, changed so two l-words do not bump together.

Because se can mean to him, to her, to you (formal) or to them, Spanish often adds a clarifying phrase: "Se lo doy a ella" (I give it to her). Two English-speaker mistakes to watch for: writing le lo, and putting the direct pronoun first (lo se doy). The chain is always se + lo/la/los/las + verb.

words.d: to him, to her, to them — what le or les becomes before lo, la, los, las: Se lo doy (I give it to him)
it to me — indirect pronoun first, then direct: Me lo preparaste (You made it for me)
it (feminine) to you — Te la mando (I send it to you)
to give — doy, das, da, damos, dais, dan; Se lo doy (I give it to him)

look.title: Shrink the Sentence
look.text:
Replace both objects with pronouns.
1. Le doy la calculadora a Tomás. → Se la doy.
2. Te mando los apuntes. → Te los mando.
3. Les compro el regalo a mis padres. → ?
4. Nos explican la lección. → ?
5. Le pido las llaves a mi mamá. → ?
look.prompt: Finish 3, 4 and 5. In which ones did le or les change to se, and why?

check.q: Which sentence correctly replaces both objects in "Le doy el libro a Ana"?
check.why: Le becomes se before lo; the indirect pronoun goes first.

check.q: What does "Te la mando" mean?
check.why: Te is to you, la is it (feminine), mando is I send.

check.q: Why is there a se in "Se los di"?
choices: Because le or les changed to se before los.
check.why: Le or les always becomes se before a direct object pronoun beginning with l.

lessons.title: Double Pronouns on the End
lessons.mainIdea: Two pronouns can attach together to an infinitive or gerund, and the longer word always takes a written accent.
reading: Both pronouns can also attach to an infinitive or a gerund, in the same order, as one word: "Voy a dártelo." (I'm going to give it to you.) "Está explicándonoslo." (She is explaining it to us.) The pronouns never split up. Either both go before the conjugated verb (Te lo voy a dar) or both go on the end (Voy a dártelo).

When two pronouns attach, a written accent is always needed, even on an infinitive. Say dar-te-lo: the stress stays on dar, now three syllables from the end, so Spanish writes *dártelo*. The same goes for comprársela (to buy it for her), decírselo (to tell it to him), and any gerund: diciéndoselo, mandándotelas. Find the syllable that was stressed in the plain verb and put the accent there.

The famous example is the command *dámelo* (give it to me), which you will meet again in the next chapter. Da is the command, me is to me, lo is it. The stress stays on da, so the accent goes there. If you can build dámelo, cómpramela and explícanoslo, you have the whole system: verb + indirect + direct, one word, accent on the original stressed syllable.

words.d: to give it to you — infinitive + te + lo, with an accent because two pronouns attached
give it to me — the command da + me + lo, accent on da
to explain — Nos lo explica / Está explicándonoslo (She is explaining it to us)
the written accent mark — keeps the stress on the same syllable when pronouns make a word longer

look.title: Syllables Before and After
look.cite: Syllable counts of the verb forms in this lesson
look.prompt: The stress stays on the same syllable every time. Which forms in the table need a written accent, and what do they have in common?

check.q: Which is written correctly?
check.why: Two attached pronouns, indirect then direct, and an accent to keep the stress on dar.

check.q: What does "Está explicándonoslo" mean?
choices: He is explaining it to them.
He is explaining it to us.
We are explaining it to him.
check.why: Nos is to us, lo is it, and estar + gerund is an action in progress.

check.q: Which pair of sentences means the same thing?
choices: Te lo voy a decir. / Voy a decírtelo.
Te lo voy a decir. / Voy a decirlo te.
Lo te voy a decir. / Voy a decírtelo.
Te lo voy a decir. / Voy a decírselo.
check.why: Both pronouns go before the conjugated verb or both attach to the infinitive, in the same order.

lessons.title: Doing It to Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: A reflexive verb sends the action back to the subject, and its pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) must match the subject.
reading: "Me ducho en tres minutos," Daniela says. Ducharse means to shower, to wash oneself. The subject (Daniela) and the object (Daniela) are the same person, so the verb is *reflexivo* (reflexive). In the dictionary a reflexive verb ends in -se: levantarse (to get up), ducharse (to shower), vestirse (to get dressed), acostarse (to go to bed).

To conjugate one, drop the -se, conjugate the verb as usual, and put the matching *pronombre reflexivo* (reflexive pronoun) in front: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan. The pronoun and the ending must agree with the same subject. "Me levanto a las seis" (I get up at six), never "Me levanta."

Some of these verbs also have stem changes, which show in all forms except nosotros and vosotros: despertarse (e → ie): me despierto, te despiertas, se despierta, nos despertamos; acostarse (o → ue): me acuesto, nos acostamos; vestirse (e → i): me visto, nos vestimos. The pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb, just like the object pronouns you already know.

words.d: reflexive — the subject does the action to itself: Me lavo (I wash myself)
the reflexive pronoun — me, te, se, nos, os, se; it matches the subject
to get up — me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan
to wake up — stem change e → ie: me despierto, nos despertamos
to go to bed — stem change o → ue: me acuesto, nos acostamos

look.title: Walk Through Ducharse
look.text:
ducharse → drop -se → duchar → conjugate → ducho, duchas, ducha, duchamos, ducháis, duchan → add the pronoun in front:
me ducho, te duchas, se ducha, nos duchamos, os ducháis, se duchan.
Now do the same with vestirse, remembering the e → i stem change in four of the six forms.
look.prompt: Write all six forms of vestirse. Which two forms keep the e of the stem, and why?

check.q: Which form is correct for "I get up"?
check.why: The reflexive pronoun me matches the yo ending -o: me levanto.

check.q: Which sentence has the right pronoun for nosotros?
check.why: Nos matches the nosotros ending -amos; nosotros has no stem change.

check.q: What does "Se despierta a las siete" mean?
choices: He or she wakes up at seven.
check.why: Se with the -a ending is the él/ella/usted form.

lessons.title: The Daily Routine
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish tells a routine with a chain of reflexive verbs and uses the definite article, not a possessive, for parts of the body and clothes.
reading: Here is Daniela's normal morning: "Me despierto a las seis, me levanto a las seis y cuarto, me ducho, me cepillo los dientes, me visto y me peino. Desayuno a las siete." (I wake up at six, get up at six fifteen, shower, brush my teeth, get dressed and comb my hair. I eat breakfast at seven.) Notice the last verb: desayunar is not reflexive, because breakfast is not done to yourself.

Look at *me cepillo los dientes* (I brush my teeth). English says "my teeth"; Spanish says "the teeth," because me already tells you whose they are. The same happens with clothes: me pongo la chaqueta (I put on my jacket), me quito los zapatos (I take off my shoes), me lavo la cara (I wash my face). Writing "mis dientes" is a common English-speaker habit; the article is the natural choice.

Some verbs change meaning when they become reflexive. Ir means to go; *irse* means to leave. Dormir means to sleep; dormirse means to fall asleep. Poner means to put; ponerse means to put on. Quedar means to remain; quedarse means to stay. "Me voy a las siete y cuarto" (I leave at seven fifteen) does not say where you are going, only that you are leaving.

words.d: to brush one's teeth — the article los, not mis, because me already shows whose
to put on (clothes) — Me pongo la chaqueta (I put on my jacket)
to take off (clothes) — Me quito los zapatos (I take off my shoes)
to leave — Me voy a las siete (I leave at seven); ir alone means to go
to fall asleep — Me duermo a las once (I fall asleep at eleven); dormir alone means to sleep
to eat breakfast — not reflexive: Desayuno a las siete

look.title: Daniela's Normal Morning
look.cite: Example schedule from the chapter story
look.prompt: Which verbs in the table are reflexive and which are not? On exam day she got up at 6:40; which steps did she probably skip?

check.q: Which is the natural way to say "I wash my face"?
check.why: The reflexive pronoun shows whose face it is, so Spanish uses the article la.

check.q: What does "Me voy" mean?
check.why: Irse, the reflexive form of ir, means to leave.

check.q: Which verb is NOT reflexive in a normal routine?
check.why: Desayunar (to eat breakfast) is not done to yourself, so it takes no reflexive pronoun.

lessons.title: Reflexive or Not?
lessons.mainIdea: The same verb is reflexive when the action stays with the subject and not reflexive when it goes to someone else.
reading: Daniela's brother wakes her up: "Mi hermano me despierta." On a normal day she wakes up by herself: "Me despierto a las seis." Both sentences have me, but they are different. In the first, me is a direct object: he wakes me. In the second, me is reflexive: I wake myself. The verb ending tells you which: despierta (he) versus despierto (I).

Many verbs work both ways. Lavar el carro (to wash the car) versus lavarse (to wash oneself). Acostar al bebé (to put the baby to bed) versus acostarse (to go to bed). Vestir a la niña (to dress the little girl) versus vestirse (to get dressed). The test: does the action land on the subject or on someone else? "La mamá viste a la niña" (the mom dresses the girl), but "La niña se viste" (the girl gets dressed).

The placement rules are the ones you already know. Before a conjugated verb: "Me quiero acostar." Attached to an infinitive: "Quiero acostarme." Attached to a gerund with an accent: "Estoy vistiéndome." The pronoun must still match the subject even when it is attached: "Vamos a levantarnos temprano" (we are going to get up early), not levantarse, because the subject is nosotros.

words.d: to wash something / to wash oneself — Lavo el carro; Me lavo las manos
to put someone to bed / to go to bed — Acuesto al bebé; Me acuesto a las diez
to dress someone / to get dressed — Viste a la niña; Se viste rápido
to get (ourselves) up — the attached pronoun still matches the subject nosotros

look.title: Same Verb, Two Directions
look.text:
1. Mi mamá despierta a mi hermano. (My mom wakes my brother.)
2. Mi hermano se despierta solo. (My brother wakes up on his own.)
3. Lavo los platos. (I wash the dishes.)
4. Me lavo las manos. (I wash my hands.)
5. Voy a acostar al perro. / Voy a acostarme.
In each pair, where does the action land?
look.prompt: Write one pair of your own with vestir / vestirse. What decides whether the pronoun appears?

check.q: Which sentence means "I put the baby to bed"?
check.why: The action goes to the baby, not back to the subject, so no reflexive pronoun is used.

check.q: Which attached pronoun is correct: "Vamos a ___ temprano"?
check.why: The subject is nosotros (vamos), so the reflexive pronoun must be nos.

check.q: In "Mi hermano me despierta," what is me?
check.why: The brother does the action to me; the subject and object are different people, so me is a direct object.

lessons.title: Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: With a plural subject, nos, os and se can mean each other, and context or el uno al otro makes it clear.
reading: On the bus Tomás says, "Nos ayudamos siempre" (we always help each other). The pronoun nos is *recíproco* (reciprocal): I help you and you help me. Reciprocal meaning only works with plural subjects, so the pronouns are nos, os and se. "Se escriben todos los días." (They write to each other every day.) "Nos vemos mañana." (We'll see each other tomorrow, a very common goodbye.)

Some of these sentences could also be reflexive. "Se miran" can mean they look at each other or they look at themselves. Usually the situation makes it obvious, but Spanish can add *el uno al otro* (each other) for reciprocal or a sí mismos (themselves) for reflexive. "Se ayudan el uno al otro." (They help each other.) "Se hablan a sí mismos." (They talk to themselves.)

Common reciprocal verbs: conocerse (to meet, to know each other), abrazarse (to hug each other), saludarse (to greet each other), quererse (to love each other), llamarse (to call each other), and verse (to see each other). "Mis abuelos se conocieron en Chicago en 1985" (My grandparents met in Chicago in 1985) is the kind of sentence you will hear in many families.

words.d: reciprocal — the action goes both ways: Nos ayudamos (we help each other)
each other — added to make the reciprocal meaning clear: Se ayudan el uno al otro
see you (we'll see each other) — a common way to say goodbye
to meet, to get to know each other — Se conocieron en Chicago (They met in Chicago)
to hug each other — Se abrazan al llegar (They hug when they arrive)

look.title: A Proverb with Te
look.text: Quien bien te quiere te hará llorar. (The one who truly loves you will make you cry.)
look.cite: Traditional Spanish proverb, origin unknown, in common use for centuries
look.prompt: Find the two pronouns te. Is either one reflexive or reciprocal? What kind of object is each?

check.q: What does "Nos escribimos cada semana" most likely mean?
choices: We write to ourselves each week.
They write to us each week.
We write to each other each week.
check.why: With a plural subject and a verb like escribir, nos is reciprocal: each other.

check.q: Which pronoun can NOT be reciprocal?
check.why: Reciprocal meaning needs a plural subject, so me (singular) cannot mean each other.

check.q: Which phrase makes "Se miran" clearly mean each other?
choices: Se miran el uno al otro.
check.why: El uno al otro means each other; a sí mismos would mean themselves.

review.why: Llaves is feminine plural, so the direct object pronoun is las.

review.q: Which sentence is in the correct order?
review.why: No goes before the pronoun, and the pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb.

review.q: Which form needs a written accent?
review.why: A gerund with an attached pronoun always takes an accent to keep its stress.

review.q: Which pronoun fills in: "___ regalo un libro a mi hermana."
review.why: Mi hermana is the person who receives the book, an indirect object: le.

review.q: How do you say "I give it (the book) to them" with two pronouns?
review.why: Les becomes se before lo; the book is singular, so lo.

review.q: Which sentence is correct for nosotros?
review.why: The reflexive pronoun nos matches the nosotros ending -amos.

review.q: What does "Se quita los zapatos" mean?
choices: He or she takes off his or her shoes.
review.why: Se with the -a ending is él/ella, and quitarse means to take off.

review.q: What does "Mis primos se llaman todos los días" mean?
choices: My cousins are named every day.
My cousins call each other every day.
My cousins call me every day.
My cousins call them every day.
review.why: With a plural subject, se is reciprocal here: each other.

chapters.title: Commands
chapters.bigQuestion: How does Spanish tell someone what to do, politely or plainly, and where do the pronouns go when it does?

story.title: Abuela's Arroz con Pollo
story.kicker: Marcos wants to cook his grandmother's rice and chicken by himself, and she coaches him by phone from Humboldt Park.
paragraphs: Marcos is seventeen and has never cooked anything harder than eggs. His grandmother's arroz con pollo (rice with chicken) is the dish every birthday in his family is built around. Tonight his parents are working late, and he wants to surprise them. He calls his abuela, who lives near Humboldt Park, and puts the phone on speaker.

"Primero, lava el pollo y sécalo bien," (First, wash the chicken and dry it well) she says. "Después, pon aceite en la olla y caliéntalo." (Then put oil in the pot and heat it.) Marcos notices something. Every instruction is a verb with no subject: lava, seca, pon, calienta. And when she wants to say "it," the pronoun sticks to the end of the verb: sécalo, caliéntalo.

He gets nervous and pours the rice in too early. "¡No lo pongas todavía!" (Don't put it in yet!) she says, hearing the sound. "No tengas prisa. Espera." (Don't be in a hurry. Wait.) Now the pronoun has jumped. In "no lo pongas" the lo is in front of the verb, and the verb itself has changed shape: pon became pongas.

His older cousin Elena walks in and starts helping. Abuela switches: "Marcos, Elena, corten la cebolla y agréguenla al pollo." (Marcos, Elena, cut the onion and add it to the chicken.) Talking to two people, she uses corten and agreguen instead of corta and agrega. Then she laughs: "Vamos a ver si les sale." (Let's see if it comes out for you.)

Forty minutes later the kitchen smells right. Marcos sends his abuela a photo. "Dime la verdad," (Tell me the truth) he writes. "¿Está bien?" She answers: "Sírvelo con limón y no le digas a tu mamá que yo te ayudé." (Serve it with lime and don't tell your mom I helped you.) He has just learned the whole system of Spanish commands over one pot of rice.
story.think: Collect every command Abuela gives. Sort them into three piles: to one person (tú), to two people (ustedes), and negative commands. What changes from pile to pile?

lessons.title: Borrowing the Él Form
lessons.mainIdea: An affirmative tú command is the same as the present-tense él/ella form of the verb.
reading: "Lava el pollo. Corta la cebolla. Come." (Wash the chicken. Cut the onion. Eat.) These are commands, and the form is called the *imperativo* (imperative). For a regular verb the affirmative tú command is simply the present-tense él/ella form: hablar → habla (speak), comer → come (eat), escribir → escribe (write). "Ella habla" and "¡Habla!" look identical; only the context and the tone differ.

Because it borrows the él form, the command keeps any stem change: cerrar → cierra (close), volver → vuelve (come back), pedir → pide (ask for), dormir → duerme (sleep). "Cierra la puerta." (Close the door.) "Vuelve pronto." (Come back soon.) English speakers sometimes use the infinitive as a command (cerrar la puerta), which sounds like a sign, not a person talking.

Spanish often softens a command with *por favor* (please) or with the person's name: "Marcos, corta la cebolla, por favor." It is also common to add the pronoun tú after the verb for emphasis: "Hazlo tú" (You do it). Tú commands are for one person you address as tú: a friend, a sibling, a classmate, a child. For a teacher or a stranger, you will use the usted forms later in this chapter.

words.d: the imperative — the command form of a verb: ¡Habla! ¡Come! ¡Escribe!
wash (tú command) — same as the él form of lavar: ella lava / ¡lava!
close (tú command) — keeps the stem change of cerrar: e → ie
please — softens a command: Corta la cebolla, por favor

look.title: From Él to Command
look.text:
hablar → él habla → ¡Habla más despacio! (Speak more slowly!)
comer → él come → ¡Come las verduras! (Eat the vegetables!)
abrir → él abre → ¡Abre la ventana! (Open the window!)
volver → él vuelve → ¡Vuelve a casa! (Come home!)
Now try: mezclar (to mix), servir (to serve), leer (to read).
look.prompt: Write the three commands. Which one has a stem change, and how did you know?

check.q: What is the affirmative tú command of comer?
check.why: The affirmative tú command matches the él/ella present form: come.

check.q: Which is the correct command: "Close the door"?
check.why: The command keeps the stem change of the él form: cierra.

check.q: Who would you naturally give a tú command to?
check.why: Tú commands are for people you address as tú: friends, siblings, cousins, classmates.

lessons.title: The Eight Irregulars
lessons.mainIdea: Eight common verbs have short one-syllable tú commands: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven.
reading: "Pon aceite en la olla." (Put oil in the pot.) Pon does not come from the él form (pone). It is one of eight *irregulares* (irregulars) that every Spanish speaker uses daily: decir → *di* (say, tell), hacer → *haz* (do, make), ir → *ve* (go), poner → *pon* (put), salir → *sal* (leave, go out), ser → *sé* (be), tener → *ten* (have), venir → *ven* (come).

Most of them are the él form with the last syllable cut off: pone → pon, tiene → ten, viene → ven, sale → sal. That trick does not work for di, haz, ve and sé, which you simply memorize. Notice the accent on sé (be): it separates the command from se the pronoun. "Sé bueno." (Be good.) "Ten paciencia." (Have patience.) "Ven aquí." (Come here.) "Haz la tarea." (Do the homework.)

Ve is doubly tricky: it is the tú command of ir (go) and also the él form of ver (to see). "Ve a la tienda" means go to the store; the a after it is your clue. English speakers often produce "hace la tarea" or "dice la verdad" as commands; those are statements (he does, he says). The commands are haz and di. Say the eight in a row until they sound like one word: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven.

words.d: say, tell (tú command of decir) — Dime la verdad (Tell me the truth)
do, make (tú command of hacer) — Haz la tarea (Do the homework)
put (tú command of poner) — Pon la mesa (Set the table)
be (tú command of ser) — Sé puntual (Be on time); the accent separates it from se
have (tú command of tener) — Ten cuidado (Be careful, literally have care)
come (tú command of venir) — Ven aquí (Come here)

look.title: A Proverb with Di
look.text: Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres. (Tell me who you walk with and I'll tell you who you are.)
look.cite: Traditional Spanish proverb, origin unknown, in common use for centuries
look.prompt: Dime is di plus me. Which of the eight irregulars is it? Why does the proverb use tú forms and not usted?

check.q: Which is the tú command of hacer?
check.why: Hacer has the irregular tú command haz; hace is a statement (he does).

check.q: What does "Ve a la tienda" tell someone to do?
check.why: Ve is the tú command of ir; ve a means go to.

check.q: Why does sé (be) carry an accent?
choices: To tell it apart from the pronoun se.
check.why: The accent distinguishes the command sé from the pronoun se.

lessons.title: Pronouns on the End
lessons.mainIdea: Object and reflexive pronouns attach to the end of an affirmative command, and an accent keeps the stress in place.
reading: "Sécalo bien." (Dry it well.) "Caliéntalo." (Heat it.) In an affirmative command, the pronoun attaches to the end of the verb as one word. Seca + lo → sécalo. Calienta + lo → caliéntalo. Compra + la → cómprala. Because the word is now longer, Spanish writes an accent on the syllable that was stressed before: SE-ca → SÉ-ca-lo.

The one-syllable irregulars also take pronouns: di + me → dime (tell me), haz + lo → hazlo (do it), pon + te → ponte (put on), ven + te → vente (come along). With one pronoun on a one-syllable command, no accent is needed. With two pronouns, the accent returns: dímelo (tell it to me), *dámelo* (give it to me), pónselo (put it on him). Indirect pronoun first, then direct, exactly as in the last chapter.

Reflexive verbs make some of the most common commands in a home: "Levántate" (get up), "Siéntate" (sit down), "Despiértate" (wake up), "Ponte los zapatos" (put on your shoes), "Lávate las manos" (wash your hands). The reflexive pronoun is always te with tú commands. A frequent mistake is writing the pronoun separately (levanta te) or forgetting the accent (levantate); both are wrong.

words.d: dry it — seca + lo, accent on sé to keep the stress
give it to me — da + me + lo; two pronouns always bring an accent
get up — the reflexive command of levantarse for tú
sit down — sentarse: stem change e → ie plus te
put on — pon + te: Ponte los zapatos (Put on your shoes)

look.title: Where the Stress Falls
look.cite: Syllable counts of the command forms in this lesson
look.prompt: In each row the stressed syllable is the same as in the plain command. When does the accent mark appear: after adding one syllable, or two, or does it depend on the word?

check.q: Which is the correct way to say "Wash them (las manos)"?
check.why: The pronoun attaches to the affirmative command and an accent keeps the stress on lá.

check.q: Which command means "Tell it to me"?
check.why: Di + me + lo in one word, indirect before direct, with an accent because two pronouns attached.

check.q: What does "Siéntate" mean?
check.why: Sentarse (to sit down) in the tú command form with the reflexive pronoun te.

lessons.title: Flip the Vowel
lessons.mainIdea: A negative tú command comes from the yo form: drop the -o, add -es for -ar verbs and -as for -er and -ir verbs.
reading: "¡No lo pongas todavía!" (Don't put it in yet!) The verb changed: pon became pongas. Negative commands do not borrow the él form. Instead they start from the present-tense *yo* form, drop the -o, and add an ending with the opposite vowel: -ar verbs take -es, and -er / -ir verbs take -as. Hablar → hablo → no hables. Comer → como → no comas. Escribir → escribo → no escribas.

Starting from the yo form matters because it carries every irregularity. Poner → pongo → *no pongas*. Tener → tengo → no tengas. Hacer → hago → no hagas. Decir → digo → no digas. Salir → salgo → no salgas. Venir → vengo → no vengas. Conocer → conozco → no conozcas. Stem changes carry over too: cerrar → cierro → no cierres; pedir → pido → no pidas.

Some verbs need a spelling change to keep the sound: -car → -ques (buscar → no busques), -gar → -gues (llegar → no llegues), -zar → -ces (empezar → no empieces). Four verbs do not end in -o in the yo form and have their own negative commands: ir → no vayas, ser → no seas, dar → no des, estar → no estés. "No seas tímido." (Don't be shy.) "No vayas solo." (Don't go alone.)

words.d: don't talk — from hablo: drop -o, add -es for an -ar verb
don't eat — from como: drop -o, add -as for an -er verb
don't put — from pongo; the yo form keeps the irregular g
don't go — ir has its own negative command
don't be — ser has its own negative command: No seas así (Don't be like that)

look.title: Build It from Yo
look.text:
tener → yo tengo → drop -o → teng- → -er verb, add -as → no tengas (don't have)
buscar → yo busco → busc- → -ar verb, add -es → spelling: no busques (don't look for)
dormir → yo duermo → duerm- → no duermas (don't sleep)
Now build: salir, empezar, pedir, venir.
look.prompt: Write the four negative commands. Which one needed a spelling change, and why is z not allowed before e?

check.q: What is the negative tú command of hacer?
check.why: Start from hago, drop -o, add -as: no hagas.

check.q: Which negative command is spelled correctly?
check.why: Llegar: llego → lleg- + es, with a u added to keep the hard g sound.

check.q: Which is the negative command of ir?
check.why: Ir has its own negative tú command: no vayas.

lessons.title: Pronouns Move to the Front
lessons.mainIdea: In a negative command every pronoun goes between no and the verb, never on the end.
reading: Compare the two sides: "Ponlo" (put it) but "No lo pongas" (don't put it). "Levántate" (get up) but "No te levantes" (don't get up). "Dímelo" (tell it to me) but "No me lo digas" (don't tell it to me). In an affirmative command the pronouns attach to the end. In a negative command they move in front of the verb, right after *no*, in the usual order: indirect, then direct.

Because the pronouns are separate words in the negative, there is never an accent to add. English speakers often keep the attached form and write "No ponlo" or "No levántate"; both break the rule. The pattern is always no + pronoun(s) + negative command verb. "No se lo digas a tu mamá." (Don't tell it to your mom.) "No te preocupes." (Don't worry.)

Some of the most useful daily phrases follow this pattern: "No te preocupes" (don't worry), "No me digas" (you don't say, no way), "No lo olvides" (don't forget it), "No te vayas" (don't leave). Try making an affirmative and a negative pair for the same idea: Cómelo / No lo comas; Hazlo / No lo hagas; Siéntate / No te sientes.

words.d: don't worry — preocuparse with te before the negative command
you don't say, no way — literally don't tell me
don't leave — irse in the negative command with te in front
don't forget it — lo goes between no and olvides

look.title: Pairs, Yes and No
look.text:
Cómpralo. / No lo compres. (Buy it. / Don't buy it.)
Dímelo. / No me lo digas. (Tell it to me. / Don't tell it to me.)
Acuéstate. / No te acuestes. (Go to bed. / Don't go to bed.)
Now make the negative of: Ponte la chaqueta. Ábrela. Dáselo.
look.prompt: Write the three negative commands. What happened to the accent marks, and why?

check.q: Which is the correct negative of "Hazlo"?
check.why: In a negative command the pronoun goes before the verb, and the verb is the negative form hagas.

check.q: What does "No te preocupes" mean?
check.why: Preocuparse means to worry; this is the negative tú command with te in front.

check.q: Which sentence follows the negative command pattern?
check.why: No + indirect (me) + direct (lo) + negative command (des).

lessons.title: Polite Commands
lessons.mainIdea: Usted and ustedes commands use the flipped-vowel form for both affirmative and negative: hable, coma, hablen, coman.
reading: A waiter to a customer: "Pase, por favor. Siéntese aquí." (Come in, please. Sit here.) A doctor to a patient: "Respire hondo." (Breathe deeply.) These are *usted* commands, for one person you address formally. They use the same flipped-vowel form as the negative tú command, minus the final -s: hablar → hable, comer → coma, escribir → escriba. And they use it whether affirmative or negative: hable / no hable.

For *ustedes*, two or more people, add -n: hablen, coman, escriban. In Latin America ustedes is the plural for everyone, formal or not, so Abuela says "corten la cebolla" to her two grandchildren. All the irregular yo-form verbs behave as expected: tenga / tengan, ponga / pongan, haga / hagan, diga / digan, salga / salgan, venga / vengan. The four special ones: vaya / vayan, sea / sean, dé / den, esté / estén.

Pronouns follow the rule you already know: attached with an accent on the affirmative, in front on the negative. "Siéntese." (Sit down.) "No se siente allí." (Don't sit there.) "Dígame." (Tell me, also how many people answer the phone in Spain.) "No me diga." (You don't say.) "Pásenlo bien." (Have a good time, to a group.) The reflexive pronoun for usted and ustedes is se.

words.d: you (formal, one person) — commands: hable, coma, escriba
you all — commands end in -n: hablen, coman, escriban
sit down (usted) — sentarse with the reflexive pronoun se attached
tell me (usted) — diga + me; a common way to answer the phone in Spain
come in, go ahead (usted) — Pase, por favor

look.title: One Verb, Four Commands
look.text:
tomar (to take):
tú: toma / no tomes
usted: tome / no tome
ustedes: tomen / no tomen
"Tome dos pastillas al día," the pharmacist says. "Tomen asiento," the teacher says to the class. "Toma, es para ti," a friend says, handing you something.
Now build the same four for volver (o → ue) and hacer.
look.prompt: Write both sets. Which forms of volver keep the stem change, and which of hacer keep the g?

check.q: Which is the usted command of comer?
check.why: Usted commands use the flipped vowel: comer → coma.

check.q: How would a teacher tell a whole class to open their books?
check.why: Ustedes commands add -n: abran.

check.q: Which is the correct negative usted command with a pronoun?
check.why: In a negative command the pronoun se goes before the verb: no se siente.

lessons.title: Let's Do It
lessons.mainIdea: Nosotros commands mean let's and end in -emos or -amos, with vamos as the everyday form for let's go.
reading: "Vamos a ver si les sale," Abuela says: let's see. When the speaker includes herself in the command, Spanish uses the *nosotros* command, which means let's. It is built with the same flipped-vowel form: -ar verbs take -emos, -er and -ir verbs take -amos. Hablar → hablemos (let's talk). Comer → comamos (let's eat). Escribir → escribamos (let's write).

For let's go, Spanish uses plain *vamos* in the affirmative, not vayamos. "¡Vamos!" (Let's go!) In the negative it switches back: "No vayamos." (Let's not go.) The very common phrase vamos a + infinitive also means let's: "Vamos a comer" (let's eat), "Vamos a empezar" (let's begin). Both comamos and vamos a comer are correct; the vamos a form is more casual in speech.

One spelling detail: when the reflexive pronoun nos attaches to an affirmative nosotros command, the final -s drops before it. Sentemos + nos → *sentémonos* (let's sit down), not sentémosnos. Levantemos + nos → levantémonos (let's get up). Vamos + nos → vámonos (let's leave), one of the most useful words in the language. The accent appears because the word got longer.

words.d: let's talk — the nosotros command of hablar: -ar → -emos
let's eat — the nosotros command of comer: -er → -amos
let's go — the affirmative nosotros command of ir; also we go
let's leave — vamos + nos with the -s dropped and an accent added
let's sit down — sentemos + nos with the -s dropped

look.title: Suggest a Plan
look.text:
A: Tengo hambre. (I'm hungry.)
B: Comamos algo. ¿Pizza? (Let's eat something. Pizza?)
A: No, no comamos pizza otra vez. Vamos a la taquería. (No, let's not eat pizza again. Let's go to the taco place.)
B: Buena idea. ¡Vámonos! (Good idea. Let's go!)
Find every nosotros command in the dialogue.
look.prompt: Which command is negative, and which one has a reflexive pronoun attached? Add one more line to the dialogue with a new let's command.

check.q: Which means "Let's write"?
check.why: Escribir is an -ir verb, so the nosotros command ends in -amos: escribamos.

check.q: Which is the usual way to say "Let's go!" in the affirmative?
check.why: Ir uses vamos for the affirmative let's go; vayamos is only for the negative.

check.q: Why is it sentémonos and not sentémosnos?
choices: Because nos is a direct object.
Because the -s drops before nos on a nosotros command.
Because the accent replaces the s.
check.why: Spanish drops the final -s of the nosotros command before the reflexive pronoun nos.

lessons.title: The Whole Command Map
lessons.mainIdea: All commands except affirmative tú use the flipped-vowel form, and pronouns attach only to affirmative commands.
reading: Step back and look at the whole map for one verb, decir (to say). Affirmative tú: di. Negative tú: no digas. Usted: diga / no diga. Ustedes: digan / no digan. Nosotros: digamos / no digamos. Only one square on the map is different from the rest: the affirmative tú command, which borrows the él form or one of the eight irregulars. Every other square uses the flipped-vowel form built from yo.

The pronoun rule is even simpler: affirmative commands take pronouns on the end (with an accent when needed); negative commands take them in front, after no. Dígamelo / No me lo diga. Levántense / No se levanten. Sentémonos / No nos sentemos. Once you see the map, a new verb is not a new problem. Find its yo form, flip the vowel, and you have five of the six squares.

This flipped-vowel form has a name you will meet in the next unit: the *presente de subjuntivo* (present subjunctive). Commands are one of its jobs. That is why no hables, hable, hablen and hablemos all look alike. Learning commands well now means most of the subjunctive forms are already in your hands before you learn what else they do.

words.d: the flipped-vowel commands of decir — all built from the yo form digo
the present subjunctive — the flipped-vowel form that commands share; its other uses come in the next unit
tell it to me (usted) — diga + me + lo with an accent
get up (ustedes) — levanten + se with an accent

look.title: Fill the Map
look.text:
hacer (to do, make):
tú: haz / no hagas
usted: haga / no haga
ustedes: hagan / no hagan
nosotros: hagamos / no hagamos
Now with the pronoun lo (it): hazlo / no lo hagas; hágalo / no lo haga; háganlo / no lo hagan; hagámoslo / no lo hagamos.
look.prompt: Build the same map for poner with the pronoun la. Which square is the odd one out, and where do the accents appear?

check.q: Which command form is NOT built from the yo form?
check.why: The affirmative tú command haz is irregular; the others come from hago.

check.q: Which is the ustedes command for "Get up"?
check.why: Ustedes: levanten + se, with an accent on the original stressed syllable.

check.q: Which pair is correct for usted: affirmative and negative of "give it to me"?
check.why: Usted uses dé; pronouns attach on the affirmative and go in front on the negative.

lessons.title: Reading a Recipe
lessons.mainIdea: Written recipes in Spanish use usted commands or infinitives, while a person coaching you out loud uses tú commands.
reading: Open a Spanish-language cookbook or a recipe card, and the verbs look different from Abuela's phone call. "Lave el pollo. Caliente el aceite. Agregue la cebolla y sofría cinco minutos." (Wash the chicken. Heat the oil. Add the onion and sauté five minutes.) Written recipes usually speak to the reader as usted, or they use bare infinitives like a list: lavar, calentar, agregar, sofreír.

The measurement words matter as much as the verbs. *Una taza* (a cup), una cucharada (a tablespoon), una cucharadita (a teaspoon), un diente de ajo (a clove of garlic), una pizca de sal (a pinch of salt). Cooking verbs you will see constantly: *mezclar* (to mix), *hervir* (to boil, e → ie: hierva), freír (to fry), picar (to chop), revolver (to stir, o → ue: revuelva), tapar (to cover), *dejar reposar* (to let rest).

Arroz con pollo is cooked across the Spanish-speaking world, and every country and every family makes it a little differently: with saffron or annatto for color, with beer or with broth, with peas or without. When you read a recipe from Puerto Rico and one from Peru, the commands are the same forms, but the ingredients tell you where the cook is from.

words.d: a cup — Agregue dos tazas de arroz (Add two cups of rice)
to mix — mezcle (usted) / mezcla (tú)
to boil — stem change e → ie: hierva (usted) / hierve (tú)
to let rest — Deje reposar cinco minutos (Let it rest five minutes)
a pinch — una pizca de sal (a pinch of salt)

look.title: Arroz con Pollo, Example Amounts
look.cite: A simple example recipe written for this lesson; real family recipes vary
look.prompt: Write the recipe as five usted commands using these amounts (Agregue dos tazas de arroz...). Then rewrite the first two as tú commands, as if you were talking to a friend.

check.q: Which is a typical written-recipe form?
check.why: Written recipes usually use usted commands: hierva.

check.q: What does "una cucharadita" mean?
check.why: Cucharadita is the small spoon, a teaspoon; cucharada is a tablespoon.

check.q: What does "Deje reposar diez minutos" tell the cook to do?
check.why: Dejar reposar means to let rest; deje is the usted command.

lessons.title: Giving Directions
lessons.mainIdea: Directions to a stranger use usted commands like siga, doble and cruce, plus a few fixed place words.
reading: A visitor in Pilsen asks, "Perdón, ¿dónde está la biblioteca?" (Excuse me, where is the library?) You answer a stranger with usted commands: "*Siga* derecho dos cuadras. *Doble* a la izquierda en la esquina. *Cruce* la calle. Está a la derecha." (Go straight two blocks. Turn left at the corner. Cross the street. It's on the right.)

The verbs are the usual flipped-vowel forms with their spelling changes: seguir → sigo → siga; doblar → doble; cruzar → cruzo → cruce (z → c before e); subir → suba; bajar → baje. The direction words: *a la derecha* (to the right), *a la izquierda* (to the left), derecho or todo recto (straight ahead), *la cuadra* (the block), la esquina (the corner), el semáforo (the traffic light).

To a friend you switch to tú: "Sigue derecho, dobla a la izquierda, cruza la calle." The negative warns: "No cruces aquí" (don't cross here), "No doble todavía" (don't turn yet, formal). Watch the pair derecho / derecha: derecho means straight ahead, and a la derecha means to the right. English speakers mix them constantly, and one wrong letter sends someone the wrong way.

words.d: continue, go on (usted) — from seguir: sigo → siga; Siga derecho (Go straight)
turn (usted) — Doble a la izquierda (Turn left)
cross (usted) — from cruzar with the z → c spelling change
to the right — not derecho, which means straight ahead
to the left — Doble a la izquierda en la esquina
the block — Siga dos cuadras (Go two blocks)

look.title: From the Bus Stop
look.text:
Un turista: Perdón, ¿cómo llego al museo? (Excuse me, how do I get to the museum?)
Tú: Siga derecho tres cuadras. En el semáforo, doble a la derecha. Cruce la calle y suba la escalera. El museo está a la izquierda.
Un turista: ¿No doblo en la esquina? (Don't I turn at the corner?)
Tú: No, no doble en la esquina. Doble en el semáforo.
look.prompt: Rewrite the directions as if you were talking to a friend (tú). Then draw the route in words: how many turns, and in which directions?

check.q: Which means "Turn left" to a stranger?
check.why: Usted command doble; a la izquierda is to the left.

check.q: What does "Siga derecho" mean?
check.why: Derecho means straight ahead; a la derecha would be to the right.

check.q: Which is the correct usted command of cruzar?
check.why: Cruzar → cruzo → cruce, with z changing to c before e.

review.q: Which is the affirmative tú command of escribir?
review.why: Affirmative tú commands match the él form: escribe.

review.q: Which of these is one of the eight irregular tú commands?
review.why: Ten is the irregular tú command of tener; the others are regular él forms.

review.q: Which is correct: "Don't tell it to her"?
review.why: Negative: no + se (from le) + lo + digas.
The reflexive pronoun attaches and an accent keeps the stress on -ván-.

review.q: Which form is the usted command of hacer?
review.why: Usted commands use the flipped-vowel form from hago: haga.
The nosotros command of an -er verb ends in -amos: comamos.

review.q: Which sentence tells a stranger to go straight?
review.why: Usted command siga; derecho means straight ahead.

review.q: Which form would you expect in a written recipe?
review.why: Written recipes usually address the reader as usted: mezcle.
